mcq.q: Under the Indian Contract Act, 1872, "an agreement enforceable by law" is the definition of a:
options: Agreement — Section 2(e)
Contract — Section 2(h)
Promise — Section 2(b)
Void agreement — Section 2(g)
mcq.explain: Section 2(h) defines a contract as an agreement enforceable by law. Section 2(e) treats an agreement as a promise, or a set of promises, supported by mutual consideration, and Section 2(g) says an agreement not enforceable by law is void. So every contract is an agreement, but not every agreement is a contract.
mcq.fast: "Enforceable by law" is the key phrase of 2(h). Agreement + enforceability = contract.

mcq.q: A shop displays a saree with a price tag of ₹4,500. Rani picks it up and goes to the counter, but the shopkeeper refuses to sell. Which is correct?
options: The display is an offer; the shopkeeper is bound to sell
The display is only an invitation to offer; Rani made the offer, which the shopkeeper may refuse
Rani accepted the offer by picking up the saree
A contract arose when Rani entered the shop
mcq.explain: Goods displayed with price tags are an invitation to offer, not an offer (Pharmaceutical Society of Great Britain v. Boots). The customer makes the offer at the counter and the shopkeeper may accept or reject it. Since no acceptance was given, no contract arose and Rani cannot compel the sale.
mcq.topic: Rules of a valid offer — and what is not an offer
mcq.fast: Price tags, catalogues, menus, tenders invited = invitation to offer. The customer offers.

mcq.q: Arun offers to sell his scooter to Bina for ₹60,000. Bina replies, "I accept if you reduce it to ₹55,000." Arun refuses. Bina then says she accepts at ₹60,000. Is there a contract?
options: Yes — at ₹60,000, since Bina finally accepted
No — Bina's reply was a counter-offer that rejected the original offer, so nothing remained to accept
Yes — at ₹57,500, the average
mcq.explain: Under Section 7 acceptance must be absolute and unqualified. A conditional reply is a counter-offer, and a counter-offer rejects the original offer (Hyde v. Wrench). Arun's offer therefore came to an end; Bina's later "acceptance" is only a fresh offer that Arun is free to refuse.
mcq.fast: Counter-offer kills the original offer. Later "acceptance" = new offer.

mcq.q: Under Section 4, when does the communication of an acceptance bind the proposer?
options: When the acceptor dispatches it and can no longer recall it
When the proposer reads it
When the proposer replies to it
When the acceptor decides to accept
mcq.explain: Section 4 splits the moment: the proposer is bound once the acceptor posts the acceptance and can no longer recall it; the acceptor is bound only when the proposer actually learns of it. That is why the acceptor can still revoke his acceptance before it reaches the proposer.
mcq.fast: Against proposer = posting. Against acceptor = proposer's knowledge.

mcq.q: Karan posts an offer on 1 May. Leela posts her acceptance on 3 May; it reaches Karan on 6 May. Karan sends a revocation of his offer on 4 May, which reaches Leela on 5 May. Which is correct?
options: The revocation is valid because it reached Leela before her acceptance reached Karan
The revocation is too late: a contract was made on 3 May when Leela posted her acceptance
No contract, since Karan had not received the acceptance
The contract is voidable at Karan's option
mcq.explain: Section 5 lets the proposer withdraw his offer only until the acceptance binds him. Under Section 4 that happened on 3 May, when Leela posted her letter. A revocation sent on 4 May is therefore too late, and a binding contract exists.
mcq.fast: Proposer can revoke only before acceptance is POSTED. Compare the revocation date with the posting date.

mcq.q: An offer made to the world at large, which can be accepted by anyone who performs its conditions, is a:
options: Specific offer
General offer
Cross offer
Counter offer
mcq.explain: A general offer is made to the public at large, such as a reward for returning a lost dog. Under Section 8 anyone who performs the conditions with knowledge of the offer accepts it (Carlill v. Carbolic Smoke Ball Co.). A specific offer is made to a definite person, and cross offers are identical offers that cross each other.
mcq.fast: Offer to "anyone/the public" = general offer, accepted by doing the act.

mcq.q: Ravi finds a lost child and brings him home, not knowing that the father had announced a reward. Later he learns of the reward and claims it. Ravi will:
options: Succeed — because he performed the act
Fail — there can be no acceptance of an offer one does not know about
Succeed — under Section 70 as a quasi contract
Get half the reward
mcq.explain: Acceptance needs knowledge of the offer; performance done in ignorance of it is not acceptance (Lalman Shukla v. Gauri Dutt). Ravi did the act before he knew of the reward, so no contract arose. Section 70 does not help him either, because he did not act intending to be paid.
mcq.fast: Did he know of the offer when he acted? No knowledge = no acceptance.

options: An offer must be communicated to the offeree
A mere statement of the lowest price is not an offer
Terms of an offer must be definite
Silence of the offeree amounts to acceptance if the offeror says so
mcq.explain: The offeror cannot turn the offeree's silence into acceptance by saying "if I hear nothing, I shall take it as accepted" (Felthouse v. Bindley). The other statements are correct rules: an offer must be communicated, a quotation of price is not an offer (Harvey v. Facey), and the terms must be certain.
mcq.topic: Rules of a valid offer — and what is not an offer
mcq.fast: Silence ≠ acceptance — the offeror cannot impose it.

mcq.q: An agreement that was enforceable when made but later becomes unenforceable because of a change in law becomes:
options: A voidable contract
An illegal agreement from the start
A void contract — Section 2(j)
An unenforceable contract that revives later
mcq.explain: Section 2(j): once a valid contract stops being enforceable, from that moment it is void. The agreement was valid when made, so it was not void from the start; it becomes void later, for example because performance becomes unlawful under a new law.
mcq.fast: Valid at birth, unenforceable later = void contract (2(j)).
